title: On the Importance of Gradients for Detecting Distributional Shifts in\n the Wild
abstract:
Detecting out-of-distribution (OOD) data has become a critical component in
ensuring the safe deployment of machine learning models in the real world.
Existing OOD detection approaches primarily rely on the output or feature space
for deriving OOD scores, while largely overlooking information from the
gradient space. In this paper, we present GradNorm, a simple and effective
approach for detecting OOD inputs by utilizing information extracted from the
gradient space. GradNorm directly employs the vector norm of gradients,
backpropagated from the KL divergence between the softmax output and a uniform
probability distribution. Our key idea is that the magnitude of gradients is
higher for in-distribution (ID) data than that for OOD data, making it
informative for OOD detection. GradNorm demonstrates superior performance,
reducing the average FPR95 by up to 16.33% compared to the previous best
method.

claims.text: GradNorm detects out-of-distribution inputs using the vector norm of gradients backpropagated from the KL divergence between softmax output and a uniform probability distribution.
Gradient magnitude derived from KL divergence with a uniform target is higher for in-distribution data than for out-of-distribution data.
GradNorm reduces average FPR95 by 16.33% compared to Energy score on the ImageNet OOD detection benchmark using ResNetv2-101.
The L1-norm of gradients in the weight matrix mathematically decomposes into the product of the feature vector norm and an output space term.
Extracting gradients from the last fully connected layer yields lower average FPR95 than extracting gradients from shallower network blocks or all parameters.
L1-norm achieves lower average FPR95 for GradNorm compared to higher-order Lp-norms and fraction norms.

limitations.text: Increasing model capacity and overparameterization degrades GradNorm performance by making gradients less distinguishable between ID and OOD data.
Existing OOD detection approaches primarily rely on output or feature space, leaving the gradient space underexplored.
Feature-based methods like Mahalanobis distance require collecting representations over the entire training set, introducing significant computational overhead on large-scale datasets.

future_work.text: Combining information obtainable from the gradient space and the output space to build a stronger OOD detection method.
